newsitem.title: USA: BOXING-LEWIS LOOKING TO REWRITE HISTORY AGAINST MCCALL.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-LEWIS LOOKING TO REWRITE HISTORY AGAINST MCCALL.

text.p: It's the winners' version of history that often gets written, and if Lennox Lewis captures the World Boxing Council heavyweight crown against Oliver McCall on Friday he intends to assert his perk and rewrite the past.
In the world according to Lewis, McCall never knocked him silly two years ago, never exposed him as a one-trick pony -- a fighter with only a good right hand.
It's very important to Lewis, as it is to many fighters, to exorcise doubts, start over, find reasons why a loss was an aberration likely to re-occur as often as Don King has a good hair day.

"Once I beat Oliver McCall and take that little glitch that was in my armour out of it, I'm saying to the world that was a lucky punch. He's my only loss, I came back and I beat him. Basically, I'm saying 'boy I don't have no losses out there. Everybody else has a loss,'" Lewis said on Tuesday.
Scoring that low in reality testing is crucial to Lewis and his supporters as they prepare for his scheduled 12-round fight with McCall (28-6).
It's called psychology 101: Don't admit to defeat so when you face your nemesis again your subconscious won't flirt with an urge to repeat history.

The Lewis company line to prepare their man for McCall, 31, is that McCall landed a lucky punch back in September 1994, and that Lewis could have continued but for a quick-triggered referee who stopped the bout.
But it certainly appeared to many onlookers that when a Jello-legged Lewis got up and wobbled into the referee a gentle breeze could have been fatal.

It was that loss and what Lewis said was a growing disrespect for trainer Pepe Correa that pushed Lewis to fire him and hire Emanuel Steward in a bid to learn more about boxing than simply loading up to land a right hand, the only effective weapon Lewis had.

The 31-year-old Briton, a 5-1 favourite against McCall who is in yet another drug rehabilitation programme as he trains for this fight, said Steward has made a tremendous difference, such as improving his balance, "different combination punches, movement, a lot of different things."
One of the biggest learning experiences for Lewis was his majority decision last May in Madison Square Garden over a very tough Ray Mercer, whom many thought actually won their slugfest.
That Lewis actually slugged it out was a surprise for many people who often criticised him for refusing to fight inside and pressing his opponent only when he thought he had him hurt.
More than a few people agreed with Mercer's assessment of Lewis before their fight.
"When he comes forward right at the start, he's gonna come like he always does -- fighting scared. He's the kind of fighter who has to get his nerve up as the rounds go by," Mercer said.

Mercer was "mentally strong and physically tough," Lewis said. "He kind of brought me out and made me fight a bit more. Basically, this was a fight that was preparing me for Mike Tyson or Oliver McCall. I look at it as gaining something."

It opened Steward's eyes, too. The veteran trainer, who guided McCall to victory over Lewis two years ago, said he saw a toughness in Lewis that made the trainer believe Lewis would be "one of the all-time great fighters."

Steward, of course, is no stranger to hyperbole, but he has a track record of training champions, such as Thomas Hearns, and it was Steward who guided Evander Holyfield to his upset victory over Riddick Bowe to win the world heavyweight title.
But, still, it seems by most measures that Lewis, 29-1, has a long way to go before he can be elevated into anyone's pantheon of pugilism.
But Steward is insistent in his nomination.
In the Mercer fight, both of Lewis's eyes "were closing up fast and his mouth was bleeding inside, and he's gotta go out and fight (not box) this guy for two more rounds," Steward said.
Lewis "got up and said 'pull my gloves up tight' and he went out there and won the last two rounds," Steward said.

"All fighters are going to have to face that sooner or later. You're not going to win all your fights on talent. But he came back and did what he had to do. And that's what makes great fighters," Steward said.
"I think he passed his test of his chin and being able to motivate himself inside without having the support of a crowd behind him. I think now he's matured as a fighter."
And now it's on to rewriting history.
